Problem 452. Reasoning with uncertain intervals: case 2
Measurements and historical dates can be uncertain. An interval represents a range of possibilities rather than one exact number.
Two measurements are uncertain intervals. A is between 9 and 13. B is between 12 and 16. A statement “A is definitely greater than B” is valid only if A’s minimum is greater than B’s maximum.
For a definite comparison under interval uncertainty, test the worst cases. Overlapping intervals usually prevent a strict guaranteed ordering.
Can we conclude that A is definitely greater than B? What comparison is justified?
1. A minimum=9, maximum=13; B minimum=12, maximum=16. 2. Test A_min > B_max: 9>16 is False. 3. If false, at least one allowed pair of values defeats the “definitely greater” claim.
No. The intervals do not justify saying A is definitely greater than B.
Robust conclusions must remain true across all values allowed by the uncertainty.

Problem 456. Counterfactual intervention: close the gate
Counterfactual reasoning asks what the model predicts if one condition were changed while the rest of the causal structure is held fixed.

Causal rules for a simplified town model: heavy rain → high river; high river AND unclosed gate → flooded square; flooded square → market closes. Actual facts: heavy rain occurred and the gate was not closed. Cross-domain check: on a field sketch, 1 cm represents 3 km and two checkpoints are 3 cm apart.

A counterfactual intervention changes one specified fact and then recomputes consequences from the rules. Keep all other stated rules the same unless the intervention changes them. For the cross-domain check, real distance = sketch distance × kilometres per centimetre.
Under the intervention “close the gate”, what changes in the consequences? Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?

1. Actual chain gives high river, then flood, then market closure. 2. Intervene: set gate=closed. 3. The flood rule requires an unclosed gate, so flooding no longer follows. 4. Without flooding, market closure does not follow. Cross-domain check: 3×3=9 km.
With the gate closed, the model no longer implies flooding or market closure. Cross-domain answer: 9 km.
A counterfactual is not ordinary storytelling; it is a controlled change followed by recomputation.
Structural causal rules with a do-style intervention on one variable.
Problem 457. Counterfactual intervention: remove heavy rain
Counterfactual reasoning asks what the model predicts if one condition were changed while the rest of the causal structure is held fixed.

Causal rules for a simplified town model: heavy rain → high river; high river AND unclosed gate → flooded square; flooded square → market closes. Actual facts: heavy rain occurred and the gate was not closed. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 8:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break.

A counterfactual intervention changes one specified fact and then recomputes consequences from the rules. Keep all other stated rules the same unless the intervention changes them. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration.
Under the intervention “remove heavy rain”, what changes in the consequences? Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish?

1. Intervene: heavy rain=false. 2. Then high river is not generated by the first rule. 3. Without high river, flooding and market closure are not generated. Cross-domain check: 8+2=10, so the team finishes at 10:00.
Without heavy rain, the model generates neither high river, flood, nor market closure. Cross-domain answer: 10:00.
A counterfactual is not ordinary storytelling; it is a controlled change followed by recomputation.

Problem 458. Counterfactual intervention: keep gate open
Counterfactual reasoning asks what the model predicts if one condition were changed while the rest of the causal structure is held fixed.

Causal rules for a simplified town model: heavy rain → high river; high river AND unclosed gate → flooded square; flooded square → market closes. Actual facts: heavy rain occurred and the gate was not closed. Cross-domain check: a local committee has 16 members, requires at least 9 present for quorum, and 14 are present.

A counterfactual intervention changes one specified fact and then recomputes consequences from the rules. Keep all other stated rules the same unless the intervention changes them. For the cross-domain check, quorum exists when present members ≥ the stated threshold.
Under the intervention “keep gate open”, what changes in the consequences? Cross-domain check: is quorum met?
1. Gate already remains open. 2. Heavy rain gives high river. 3. High river plus open gate gives flood, then market closure. Cross-domain check: compare 14 with 9; 14≥9 is true.
The original chain remains: flood and market closure occur. Cross-domain answer: quorum is met.
A counterfactual is not ordinary storytelling; it is a controlled change followed by recomputation.

Problem 459. Counterfactual intervention: prevent high river
Counterfactual reasoning asks what the model predicts if one condition were changed while the rest of the causal structure is held fixed.

Causal rules for a simplified town model: heavy rain → high river; high river AND unclosed gate → flooded square; flooded square → market closes. Actual facts: heavy rain occurred and the gate was not closed. Cross-domain check: researchers collected 15 reports, but 4 are exact duplicate copies that add no new independent information.

A counterfactual intervention changes one specified fact and then recomputes consequences from the rules. Keep all other stated rules the same unless the intervention changes them. For the cross-domain check, independent reports = total reports − duplicate copies.
Under the intervention “prevent high river”, what changes in the consequences? Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain?

1. Intervene directly: high river=false. 2. Even with rain, the counterfactual intervention fixes high river as prevented for this question. 3. Flood requires high river, so it does not follow. Cross-domain check: 15−4=11 independent reports remain.
Preventing the high river blocks the flood and market closure in this model. Cross-domain answer: 11 independent reports.
A counterfactual is not ordinary storytelling; it is a controlled change followed by recomputation.
